title: Building a Production RAG Pipeline
summary: A production RAG system needs more than basic retrieval: careful chunking, hybrid keyword+vector search, reranking to surface the best chunks, and evaluation to measure quality. Today you assemble these into a robust pipeline and learn to measure whe
content:
# Building a Production RAG Pipeline ##### The error code that semantic search could not find The Pune legal-tech team from Day 35 shipped their RAG system and it worked well — until the support team started using it too. An engineer asked: *"What causes error ERR_GST_4021 during invoice upload?"* The system returned three chunks about general GST compliance, none mentioning the error code. The answer was useless. Yet the troubleshooting guide in the corpus had a section titled exactly "ERR_GST_4021 — Invalid GSTIN checksum." **The embedding for `ERR_GST_4021` is close to nothing**, because the string carries no semantic content. It is an opaque token. Meanwhile BM25 keyword search would have found it instantly on exact match. They added hybrid search. That query started working, and overall retrieval recall went from 0.71 to 0.86. Then they added a reranker, and it went to 0.93. Day 35 gave you a RAG system that works. Today makes it one you can put in front of users — through better ingestion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and, most importantly, **measurement**. ##### The production architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph ING["Ingestion pipeline"] A["Documents"] --> B["Extract + clean
preserve structure"] B --> C["Structure-aware chunking"] C --> D["Enrich metadata
section, date, access"] D --> E["Embed"] E --> F[("Vector index")] D --> G[("BM25 index")] end subgraph RET["Retrieval — every query"] H["Query"] --> I["Vector search
top-25"] H --> J["BM25 search
top-25"] F --> I G --> J I --> K["Reciprocal Rank Fusion"] J --> K K --> L["Cross-encoder reranker
25 → top-5"] L --> M["Assemble prompt"] M --> N["LLM"] N --> O["Answer + citations"] end O --> P["Log: query, chunks,
answer, latency, cost"] P --> Q["RAGAS evaluation"] ``` Three additions to Day 35: a second retrieval path, a fusion-plus-rerank stage, and a measurement loop. ##### Advanced chunking Fixed-size splitting ignores document structure. Production ingestion respects it. **Structure-aware chunking** splits at headings first, then within sections: ```python from langchain_text_splitters import (MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter) header_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter( headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2"), ("###", "h3")], strip_headers=False, ) body_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=900, chunk_overlap=150, separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""], ) sections = header_splitter.split_text(markdown_text) chunks = [] for section in sections: for piece in body_splitter.split_documents([section]): # Prepend the heading trail so each chunk is self-describing trail = " > ".join( v for k, v in piece.metadata.items() if k.startswith("h") ) piece.page_content = f"[{trail}]\n\n{piece.page_content}" chunks.append(piece) ``` **Prepending the heading trail is a small change with a large effect.** A chunk reading "The limit is ₹5,000 per day" is nearly useless in isolation. The same chunk prefixed with `[Health Policy 2026 > Room Rent > Sub-limits]` is retrievable and interpretable. **Other techniques worth knowing:** - **Contextual retrieval** (Anthropic, 2024) — use a cheap LLM to write a one-sentence context for each chunk describing where it sits in the document, and prepend it before embedding. Reported ~35% reduction in retrieval failures. Costs one small LLM call per chunk at ingestion, once. - **Parent-document retrieval** — embed small precise chunks for matching, but return the larger parent section to the LLM. Best of both: precise retrieval, complete context. - **Table and code handling** — never split a table mid-row. Extract tables separately and store them whole, with a text summary for embedding. ##### Hybrid search Day 33's comparison, now implemented. BM25 (keyword) and vector search fail on different queries, so run both. ```python import numpy as np from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi import re def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]: return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()) class HybridRetriever: def __init__(self, chunks, metadatas, embedder, collection): self.chunks = chunks self.metadatas = metadatas self.embedder = embedder self.collection = collection self.bm25 = BM25Okapi([tokenize(c) for c in chunks]) def _vector_ids(self, query, k): res = self.collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=k, include=["metadatas"]) return [m["global_index"] for m in res["metadatas"][0]] def _bm25_ids(self, query, k): scores = self.bm25.get_scores(tokenize(query)) return list(np.argsort(-scores)[:k]) def search(self, query, k=5, candidates=25, rrf_k=60): vec_ranked = self._vector_ids(query, candidates) kw_ranked = self._bm25_ids(query, candidates) # Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank) fused: dict[int, float] = {} for ranked in (vec_ranked, kw_ranked): for rank, idx in enumerate(ranked, start=1): fused[idx] = fused.get(idx, 0.0) + 1.0 / (rrf_k + rank) top = sorted(fused, key=fused.get, reverse=True)[:k] return [{"text": self.chunks[i], "metadata": self.metadatas[i], "rrf_score": round(fused[i], 5)} for i in top] ``` **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** is the standard way to combine ranked lists, and its virtue is that it uses only *ranks*, not scores. This matters because BM25 scores are unbounded and cosine similarities live in [−1, 1] — they are not comparable, and naively weighting them requires per-corpus tuning that breaks whenever your data changes. RRF sidesteps the problem entirely. The constant `k=60` comes from the original RRF paper and works well without tuning. It damps the influence of rank differences deep in the list. | Query type | Vector wins | BM25 wins | |---|---|---| | "how do I get a refund" | ✓ | | | "ERR_GST_4021" | | ✓ | | "stomach ache remedies" | ✓ | | | "Clause 8.1" | | ✓ | | "what if my package is late" | ✓ | | | "IFSC HDFC0001234" | | ✓ | ##### Reranking Bi-encoders — the embedding models from Day 33 — encode query and document *separately*. That is what makes them fast, and it is also what limits their accuracy: the model never sees the two texts together. A **cross-encoder** takes `(query, document)` as a single input and outputs a relevance score. Far more accurate, far too slow to run over a whole corpus. The production pattern uses both: ``` 1.4M chunks → hybrid retrieval (fast, approximate) → 25 candidates 25 candidates → cross-encoder rerank (slow, accurate) → top 5 top 5 → LLM ``` ```python from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder reranker = CrossEncoder("BAAI/bge-reranker-base", max_length=512) def rerank(query: str, candidates: list[dict], top_k: int = 5, min_score: float = 0.0): pairs = [(query, c["text"]) for c in candidates] scores = reranker.predict(pairs, batch_size=32) for c, s in zip(candidates, scores): c["rerank_score"] = float(s) ranked = sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: -c["rerank_score"]) return [c for c in ranked if c["rerank_score"] >= min_score][:top_k] candidates = hybrid.search(query, k=25, candidates=25) final = rerank(query, candidates, top_k=5) ``` **Reranking is usually the single highest-return addition to a RAG system** — typically 10–20 points of precision for about 50–150ms of added latency on 25 candidates. Options: `BAAI/bge-reranker-base` (fast, local, free), `bge-reranker-v2-m3` (multilingual, better), and Cohere Rerank (API, excellent, paid). The reranker score is also a natural **relevance gate**. If nothing clears your threshold, refuse rather than answer from weak context — reusing Day 35's refusal path. ##### Prompt design for RAG ```python RAG_SYSTEM = """You answer questions using ONLY the provided context. Rules: 1. Use only the context. Never use prior knowledge. 2. Cite every claim as [Source N]. 3. If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: "I could not find this in the provided documents." 4. Quote exact figures, dates, clause numbers, and codes from the context. Never approximate or infer them. 5. If sources conflict, say so and cite both. 6. Be concise. Do not add caveats the context does not support.""" def build_context(chunks: list[dict], max_chars: int = 8000) -> str: """Most relevant first and last — mitigates 'lost in the middle'.""" blocks, used = [], 0 for i, c in enumerate(chunks, start=1): m = c["metadata"] block = (f"[Source {i}] {m.get('source')} " f"(page {m.get('page', '?')}, {m.get('section', '')})\n" f"{c['text']}") if used + len(block) > max_chars: break blocks.append(block) used += len(block) if len(blocks) > 2: # reorder: best at the edges ordered = [blocks[0]] + blocks[2:] + [blocks[1]] else: ordered = blocks return "\n\n---\n\n".join(ordered) ``` **That reordering is a real technique.** The "lost in the middle" finding (Liu et al., 2023) shows models attend most reliably to the start and end of a long context. Placing your two best chunks at the extremes measurably improves answer quality. **Keep the context tight.** Five good chunks beat twenty mediocre ones — more context dilutes attention, raises cost, and increases latency. The reranker exists precisely so you can pass fewer, better chunks. ##### RAG evaluation with RAGAS You cannot improve what you do not measure, and RAG has two failure modes that need separate metrics. RAGAS decomposes quality into four: | Metric | Question | Diagnoses | |---|---|---| | **Context recall** | Did we retrieve everything needed? | **Retrieval** | | **Context precision** | Are the retrieved chunks relevant and well-ranked? | **Retrieval** | | **Faithfulness** | Is the answer supported by the context? | **Generation** (hallucination) | | **Answer relevancy** | Does the answer address the question? | **Generation** | ```python from datasets import Dataset from ragas import evaluate from ragas.metrics import (faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall) eval_data = { "question": [ "What is the notice period for terminating the MSA?", "What causes error ERR_GST_4021?", ], "answer": [], # your system's answers "contexts": [], # list of retrieved chunk texts per question "ground_truth": [ "The notice period is 90 days written notice (Clause 8.1).", "ERR_GST_4021 is raised when the GSTIN checksum is invalid.", ], } for q in eval_data["question"]: result = rag_answer(q) eval_data["answer"].append(result["answer"]) eval_data["contexts"].append([c["text"] for c in result["chunks"]]) scores = evaluate( Dataset.from_dict(eval_data), metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall], ) print(scores) ``` **Reading the results is the skill:** ``` faithfulness: 0.91 context_recall: 0.62 answer_relevancy: 0.88 context_precision: 0.71 ``` Faithfulness is high but context recall is low. **The generator is fine; retrieval is the bottleneck.** Do not touch the prompt — improve chunking, add hybrid search, or tune the reranker. The opposite pattern — recall 0.94, faithfulness 0.68 — means you are retrieving the right material and the model is embellishing. Fix the prompt, lower the temperature, or use a stronger model. **A caution:** RAGAS uses an LLM as judge, so it costs money and carries the judge's biases. Use it for relative comparison between your own versions, not as an absolute score. And always keep a small human-labelled set as ground truth. ##### Measuring your improvements Build one evaluation set and run every change against it: ```python def compare_configs(eval_set, configs): rows = [] for name, retriever in configs.items(): recalls, mrrs, latencies = [], [], [] for item in eval_set: t0 = time.perf_counter() hits = retriever(item["query"], k=5) latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) ids = [h["metadata"]["chunk_id"] for h in hits] rel = item["relevant_ids"] recalls.append(len(set(ids) & rel) / len(rel)) mrrs.append(next((1/r for r, i in enumerate(ids, 1) if i in rel), 0.0)) rows.append({"config": name, "recall@5": round(np.mean(recalls), 3), "MRR": round(np.mean(mrrs), 3), "p50_ms": round(np.percentile(latencies, 50), 1)}) return pd.DataFrame(rows) compare_configs(eval_set, { "vector only": lambda q, k: vector_search(q, k), "hybrid": lambda q, k: hybrid.search(q, k), "hybrid + rerank": lambda q, k: rerank(q, hybrid.search(q, 25), k), }) ``` A typical result: | config | recall@5 | MRR | p50_ms | |---|---|---|---| | vector only | 0.710 | 0.601 | 14.2 | | hybrid | 0.862 | 0.703 | 31.5 | | hybrid + rerank | 0.931 | 0.847 | 148.0 | That table is the deliverable. It tells you exactly what each stage bought and what it cost, and it lets you decide whether 148ms is acceptable for your product. ##### Common mistakes - **Vector search alone** for corpora containing IDs, codes, or clause numbers. - **No reranker** — usually the largest single available improvement. - **Passing twenty chunks** instead of five good ones. - **Ignoring "lost in the middle"** and putting the best chunk in the centre. - **Weighting BM25 and cosine scores directly** instead of fusing ranks with RRF. - **No evaluation set**, so every change is a guess. - **Optimising faithfulness when recall is the bottleneck** (or vice versa) — read the metrics before acting. - **Chunks with no heading context**, unintelligible in isolation. - **Not logging retrieved chunks in production**, making incident debugging impossible. - **Rebuilding the whole index for a single document update** — support incremental upserts. - **Trusting RAGAS scores absolutely** rather than as relative comparisons. - **No stale-document handling**, so superseded policies get retrieved alongside current ones. ##### Hands-on: measure each stage Your practical task adds a reranker to your Day 35 app and measures the improvement. Do it as a controlled experiment: same queries, same corpus, retrieve 25 candidates, then compare top-5 with and without reranking. Record recall@5 and latency for both. The reranker's contribution is usually large enough to be obvious, and having your own number is what makes the case for the extra 100ms. The mini project is a documentation Q&A assistant with hybrid search, reranking, citations, and a RAGAS report. Pick documentation you know well — a library you use, your college's academic regulations, or a government scheme's guidelines. Build a 25-question evaluation set *first*, before optimising anything, so you have a baseline. Then add each component and record the metrics after each addition. That progression table is the strongest part of the deliverable. The assignment evaluates with RAGAS and writes recommendations. The recommendations must follow from the numbers: if context recall is 0.6 and faithfulness is 0.9, your recommendation is about chunking and retrieval, not prompting. Write one recommendation per weak metric, each naming the specific change and the expected effect. That diagnostic reasoning — reading four numbers and knowing which lever to pull — is exactly what a senior GenAI engineer does. ##### Key takeaways - **Hybrid search fixes what embeddings cannot see** — error codes, IDs, clause numbers — and Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the two ranked lists without needing comparable scores. - **A cross-encoder reranker on 25 candidates is usually the highest-return single addition**, buying 10–20 points of precision for ~100ms. - **Chunks must be self-describing.** Prepend heading trails or contextual summaries, or a retrieved fragment means nothing on its own. - **Pass five good chunks, not twenty**, and place the best ones at the start and end of the context. - **RAGAS separates retrieval failure from generation failure** — read context recall against faithfulness before deciding whether to fix your chunking or your prompt.
